title: Can deterministic (Delta+1)-coloring beat square-root dependence on degree?
formal: Is there one deterministic LOCAL algorithm that properly colors every simple n-vertex graph of maximum degree $\Delta\ge2$ with colors in $\{1,\ldots,\Delta+1\}$ in $O(\Delta^{0.499}+\log^* n)$ synchronous rounds? Vertices have arbitrary distinct O(log n)-bit identifiers and know n and Delta. Messages along input edges and local computation are unbounded. The constant in the round bound must be independent of both n and Delta.
answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm with the specified uniform round bound, or prove that no deterministic LOCAL algorithm attains it. Improving a logarithmic factor while retaining degree exponent one-half does not meet the target.
context:
A sequential greedy algorithm needs only one more color than the maximum degree: when processing a vertex, at most Delta colors have already been used by its neighbors. In a distributed algorithm many adjacent vertices act simultaneously, so they can choose conflicting colors unless their decisions are coordinated.

Unique identifiers break perfect symmetry, but treating every identifier as a color starts with far too many colors. Color reduction has to compress this large palette while preserving a distinction across every edge. The degree controls how many simultaneous conflicts a vertex may need to avoid.

The two parameters in the target play different roles. Even when degree is fixed, the network can have arbitrarily many vertices, and iterated logarithmic time captures the unavoidable symmetry-breaking dependence on that size. An algorithm taking a power of log n cannot simply replace this term: for sufficiently large n, it exceeds every bound depending only on Delta plus log-star n.

The target chooses a specific exponent strictly below one-half, as in Suomela’s list. The numerical improvement is small; its purpose is to cross the apparent degree barrier while keeping the optimal-size palette. Allowing more colors, randomness, or a larger n-dependent term gives separate questions.
why: I include this because the familiar greedy palette bound hides a distinct distributed coordination problem. A fixed improvement in the degree exponent would reveal new ways to resolve local conflicts, while an impossibility result would explain why the square-root dependence persists across different coloring methods.
definitions: Proper coloring means adjacent vertices receive different output colors. Delta denotes a supplied upper bound on degree, and the guarantee holds for every such valid bound. The algorithm is uniform over n, Delta, and identifier assignments. Log-star n is the number of repeated base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one. Elapsed synchronous rounds are measured; this is not a sequential running-time or message-count target.

progress.text: Maus and Tonoyan obtain $O(\sqrt{\Delta\log\Delta}+\log^*n)$ deterministic rounds for the more general degree-plus-one list-coloring task. Ordinary coloring follows by using a common palette.
Suomela’s updated open-problem list explicitly asks whether the exponent 0.499 is attainable with Delta+1 colors and only an additive log-star n dependence.

The SODA 2026 discussion records a separate deterministic $\widetilde O(\log^{5/3}n)$ upper bound for Delta+1 coloring. That bound is independent of degree but does not provide the two-parameter guarantee asked here.

importance.reason: Breaking the square-root degree barrier for the canonical coloring task would improve a broadly reused distributed primitive.
